entries.topicDescription: Build variants, product flavors, and custom Gradle tasks for Android projects.

tips.title: Product flavors and build types combine to form every build variant
tips.content:
Build types (debug/release) alone only control things like
debuggability and minification, while separate concerns like
'which backend environment' or 'which app tier' (free vs paid) don't fit
naturally into that same axis.

Product flavors add a second, independent axis — Gradle automatically
combines every flavor with every build type to produce the full variant
matrix (e.g. freeDebug, freeRelease, paidDebug, paidRelease), each with
its own source set for flavor-specific code, resources, and
configuration.

tips.title: Declare dependency versions once in a version catalog
tips.content:
A version catalog (gradle/libs.versions.toml) is one file that lists every library, its version and your plugins. Modules refer to entries through generated type-safe accessors, so a version is changed in exactly one place and IDE autocomplete finds the alias.

Bundles group libraries that are always added together, and the [versions] table lets several libraries share one version number.

tips.title: Share build logic with convention plugins instead of copy-pasted blocks
tips.content:
In a multi-module project, every module ends up repeating the same compileSdk, Kotlin options and test setup. Configuring this from the root with allprojects or subprojects blocks hides where settings come from and makes builds harder to cache.

A convention plugin, written once in an included build (commonly named build-logic), holds the shared configuration, and each module just applies it by ID. The settings live in real, testable Kotlin code and stay next to the plugin that owns them.

tips.title: Turn on the build cache, configuration cache and parallel execution
tips.content:
Three switches in gradle.properties remove a lot of wasted time. The build cache reuses task outputs from earlier builds (even from other machines through a remote cache), the configuration cache skips the configuration phase when nothing that affects it changed, and parallel execution builds independent modules at the same time.

Turn them on together, and if the configuration cache reports a problem, it is usually a task or plugin reading project state at execution time.

tips.title: Declare a custom task's inputs and outputs so Gradle can cache it
tips.content:
A task is only skipped or cached if Gradle knows what it reads and writes. Annotate inputs and outputs, mark the task @CacheableTask when it is deterministic, and use PathSensitivity so cached results are reusable across machines with different checkout paths.

Avoid reading project or extension state inside the task action: pass values as declared properties, which is also what the configuration cache needs.
